      MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF'S MOTION FOR ENTRY OF A
         SCHEDULING ORDER AND, AS NECESSARY, AN INITIAL PRETRIAL
                                         CONFERENCE


 I.     INTRODUCTION
        This action has an operative complaint, appearing Defendants, and pending motions. ECF

 5, 10, 21 , 45 . It has no Rule 16(b) scheduling order. NCMEC was served on July 31, 2026, and

 appeared on August 12, 2026. ECF 3, 10. Under Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2) and 6(a), the ordinary

 deadline for the scheduling order, absent a finding of good cause for delay, was October 13, 2026.

 ECF 84 confirmed on October 7, 2026 that no scheduling order existed. ECF 84 at 1-2.

        Plaintiff requests three things. First, entry of the scheduling order after the report or

 consultation Rule 16(b)(1) requires. Second, an initial scheduling conference where necessary to

 obtain that consultation, even if the Court is not prepared to enter the complete schedule at once.

 Third, if either step is postponed, an order stating the good cause found under Rule 16(b)(2) and



                                                  1

 the date or event on which scheduling will next be addressed. The third request is not a substitute

 for the first two and is not consent to postponement.

        This Motion does not seek authorization of particular discovery, adjudication of any

 discovery dispute, or reconsideration of any ruling. It asks the Court to establish the timetable for

 a pending action.

        Three motions to dismiss are pending. ECF 10, 21, 45. Plaintiffs objections and

 applications concerning ECF 84 and ECF 96 remain pending. ECF 89, 90, 93, 97-99. None of

 those filings is the subject of this Motion.

 III.   RULE 16(b) GOVERNS THIS ACTION, AND ITS ORDINARY DEADLINE RAN
         ON OCTOBER 13, 2026.
        A.       The action is not exempt.
        Rule 16(b)(1) applies "[ e]xcept in categories of actions exempted by local rule." Fed. R.

 Civ. P. 16(b)(l). Local Civil Rule 16(A) exempts "[p]roceedings upon a defendant's default and

 matters involving habeas corpus petitions, other pro se prisoner petitions, bankruptcy proceedings,




                                                   2

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF            Document 104        Filed 10/28/26      Page 3 of 10 PageID#
                                            1062



 condemnation cases, forfeitures, and reviews from administrative agencies." E.D. Va. L. Civ. R.

 16(A). This is a civil action by a non-prisoner asserting claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2) and

 Virginia law. ECF 5. It is in none of the exempt categories. Local Civil Rule 16(B) therefore

 applies: "In all other civil actions, as promptly as possible after a complaint or notice of removal

 has been filed, the Court shall schedule an initial pretrial conference to be conducted in accordance

 with Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)." Local Civil Rule 16(B).

        B.      The computation.
        Rule 16(b)(2) provides that "unless the judge finds good cause for delay, the judge must

 issue it within the earlier of 90 days after any defendant has been served with the complaint or 60

 days after any defendant has appeared." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2). Local Civil Rule 16(B) sets the

 same outer bound: "not later than sixty (60) days from first appearance or ninety (90) days after

 service of the complaint." Local Civil Rule 16(B).

        Rule 6(a) governs the computation of "any time period specified in these rules ." Fed. R.

 Civ. P. 6(a). The 90-day interval is not a second period that opens after the 60-day period closes.

 Rule 16(b)(2) selects the earlier of the two. The ordinary Rule 16(b)(2) deadline, absent a finding

 of good cause for delay, was October 13, 2026.

                                            1063



        C.      The command and the exception.
        Rule 16(b)(2) states both. The judge "must issue" the scheduling order within the period.

 The judge may issue it later upon finding "good cause for delay." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2). Plaintiff

 does not contend that the lapse affects the Court's jurisdiction or the validity of any order entered

 since. Plaintiff does not contend that passage of the deadline itself authorizes service of discovery.

 Plaintiff contends that the period has run and that the rule now calls for one of two things: a

 scheduling order, or a finding of good cause for a defined delay.

 IV.    RULE 16(b)(l) SUPPLIES TWO ROUTES TO THE SCHEDULING ORDER,
        AND EITHER CAN BEGIN NOW.
        Rule 16(b)( 1) provides two means of proceeding: receipt of the parties' Rule 26( f) report

 or consultation with counsel and the unrepresented party at a scheduling conference. Fed. R. Civ.

 P. 16(b)(1 )(A)-(B). Plaintiff requests the conference route if a sufficient report is not available.

 Local Civil Rule 16(B) permits scheduling without a conference where the federal requirements

 are otherwise satisfied; Plaintiff does not invoke it to dispense with both alternatives.

        The parties' Rule 26(f) conference is the subject of a separate motion. Plaintiff does not

 represent here that the conference is complete, and this Motion does not depend on it.

        Where no completed report exists, Rule 16(b)(l)(B) supplies the Court' s own means of

 scheduling. Rule 26(f)(l) ties the parties' conference to the Court's calendar: the parties must

 confer "at least 21 days before a scheduling conference is to be held or a scheduling order is due

 under Rule 16(b)," except "when the court orders otherwise." Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(l). Rule 26(f)

 (4) permits a court, by local rule, to require the parties' conference to occur less than 21 days

 before the scheduling conference, to shorten the reporting interval, and to excuse the written report

 in favor of oral reporting at the Rule 16(b) conference. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(4). Local Civil Rule

 26(A)(l) adopts those adjustments for this District. Local Civil Rule 26(A)(l)(a)-(b). A



                                                   4

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF             Document 104          Filed 10/28/26       Page 5 of 10 PageID#
                                             1064



 conference-setting order that shortens the intervals supplies dates the parties can meet after the

 order issues. Plaintiff requests that order. Mot. ~ 9(c).

        The 2015 amendment to Rule 16(b)(2) shortened the scheduling timetable to reduce delay

 at the beginning of litigation. The Advisory Committee recognized that some cases require more

 time to prepare a complete schedule, and contemplated that an initial scheduling conference would

 ordinarily occur within the timetable even where final scheduling required additional time. Fed.

 R. Civ. P. 16 advisory committee's note to 2015 amendment. That distinction supports the separate

 request in Motion ~ 10: if the Court determines that the complete scheduling order should await

 another development, the Court can still hold the initial conference now and establish the

 remaining case-management steps. Plaintiff does not contend that the note entitles Plaintiff to the

 particular dates proposed.

        The party-to-party conference under Rule 26(f) and the Court's conference under Rule

 16(b) are distinct events. Plaintiff does not offer the Court's conference as a finding that the parties'

 conference has occurred. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to find that any Defendant has declined

 to participate, to require a written-only conference, or to adopt Plaintiffs proposals by default.

 Plaintiff asks the Court to set the consultation Rule 16(b)(1 )(B) describes and to direct the

 preparatory steps the Court requires.

 V.     ECF 84 IDENTIFIED THE ABSENCE OF A SCHEDULING ORDER; THIS
        MOTION REQUESTS THE PROCESS WHOSE ABSENCE IT IDENTIFIED.
        ECF 84 addressed Plaintiffs motions for limited discovery before the Rule 26(f)

 conference and Plaintiffs motion for leave to amend. ECF 15, 54, 59. It denied the discovery

 motions "as premature" and stated that "discovery officially begins when the District Judge issues

 a Scheduling Order and currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case." ECF 84 at 1-2. ECF




                                                    5

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF             Document 104        Filed 10/28/26      Page 6 of 10 PageID#
                                             1065



 84 did not set a scheduling timetable and did not make a finding of good cause for delay under

 Rule 16(b)(2).

         ECF 84 relied on the absence of a scheduling order in denying the requests before it.

 Plaintiff maintains his objections to that reasoning in the pending review applications. ECF 89, 90,

 93. This Motion presents a different request: establish the scheduling process whose absence the

 order identified. Continued absence of that process leaves no date for the next ordinary case-

 management step.

        If the Court relies on ECF 84 as a reason to defer scheduling itself, Plaintiff requests

 identification of that construction and its basis.

 VI.    PENDING MOTIONS ARE MANAGED THROUGH THE SCHEDULE, NOT
         THROUGH AN UNDEFINED POSTPONEMENT.
        Three motions to dismiss are pending. ECF 10, 21, 45. Rule 16(b)(2) measures the ordinary

 deadline from service or appearance, not from the filing of an answer. Pending motions may be

 relevant to a case-specific finding of good cause for delay, but their existence does not replace that

 determination. The first is a docket fact. The second is a determination Rule 16(b)(2) assigns to

 the judge.

        The First Amended Complaint is the operative pleading. ECF 5. Scheduling proceeds from

 the operative pleading. Rule 16(b)(3)(A) requires the scheduling order to "limit the time to join

 other parties, amend the pleadings, complete discovery, and file motions." Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)

 (3)(A). Rule 16(b)(4) permits modification "for good cause and with the judge's consent." Fed. R.

 Civ. P. 16(b)(4). Those provisions allow a schedule to be entered while motions are pending and

 adjusted when rulings issue. The Court retains its authority to sequence the case through the

 schedule it enters.




                                                      6

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF            Document 104          Filed 10/28/26      Page 7 of 10 PageID#
                                            1066



        Plaintiff does not ask the Court to predict the disposition of the pending motions. Plaintiff

 asks the Court to establish the timetable governing this action while those motions remain pending.

 If the Court determines that a pending motion supplies good cause for delay, Rule 16(b)(2)

 accommodates that determination, with the scope and duration of the postponement identified.

 This Motion does not request a stay of the motions to dismiss and does not expand any sequencing

 request already pending.

 VII.   ANY POSTPONEMENT SHOULD STATE ITS BASIS AND THE NEXT
        SCHEDULING STEP.
        Rule 16(b)(2) predicates delay on a finding of good cause. Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(2). If the

 Court postpones the scheduling conference or entry of the scheduling order, Plaintiff requests that

 the order state the good cause found and the date or event on which scheduling will next be

 addressed. A stated basis permits the parties to determine what remains required and when the

 action will proceed. The request for a stated basis is not consent to postponement and does not

 withdraw the request for scheduling now.

 VIII. CONCLUSION
        Plaintiff requests that the Court: ( 1) enter a scheduling order after the report or consultation

 Rule 16(b)( 1) requires, with the preparatory intervals shortened under Rule 26( f)(l ), Rule 26( f)

 (4), and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(l); (2) set an initial scheduling conference on a date certain if the

 Court requires one to accomplish that consultation, or if the Court determines that the complete

 scheduling order should await another development; and (3) if the Court postpones either step,

 state the good cause found under Rule 16(b)(2) and the date or event on which scheduling will

 next be addressed. Plaintiff requests disposition of each request to the extent the preceding request

 is denied or deferred.
